name: Lateral Line Pressure Sense
description: Introduces a lateral line system — a series of pressure-sensitive neuromasts — along the forearms, flanks, and calves. The system detects water currents, pressure waves, and hydrodynamic disturbances, providing underwater spatial awareness comparable to fish. In water, the user can feel the movement of other swimmers, detect obstacles by water displacement, sense current direction and strength, and navigate in zero-visibility conditions. On land, the modification provides limited benefit — it detects strong air currents and nearby movement through air pressure displacement, functioning as a crude proximity sense in a 1–2 meter radius. Combined with gills and deep-pressure resistance, the lateral line makes the user a genuinely aquatic organism. The neuromasts are visible as faint dotted lines along the installation paths.
source_organism: Astyanax mexicanus (Mexican blind cavefish, enhanced neuromast sensitivity), Clarias batrachus (walking catfish, air-functional lateral line)
procedure: Subdermal neuromast implantation along lateral paths, 3 sessions
reversibility: Neuromasts surgically removable; neural pathways persist
side_effects: Dotted lines visible along forearms and flanks
Overwhelming input during storms or in turbulent water
Sensitivity to air pressure changes — weather fronts are physically felt
Shower water becomes a sensory experience rather than a mundane activity
Rare: neuromast hypersensitivity causing phantom pressure sensations
social_perception: Aquatic-culture specific and respected. Lateral line users are serious about their aquatic life. The visible dotted lines are recognized by anyone familiar with geneware. In Old Harbor, the lines are a mark of professional capability.
story_hooks: A lateral line user in Old Harbor detects a massive pressure wave approaching from the deep harbor — something very large is moving underwater, and it's heading for the surface
A Fish Feel user discovers their neuromasts are picking up organized pressure patterns — rhythmic, deliberate signals that suggest something in the water is communicating
